newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sweden says no reason for companies to quit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sweden says no reason for companies to quit.

text.p: The Swedish government, under fire from industry for failing to stimulate the business sector, rejected the criticism on Tuesday but said it was considering easing taxation of foreign executives.

Prime Minister Goran Persson told reporters that Swedish companies were going through a period of unprecedented success. "I don't quite get it if this success is supposed to be an example of how bad the business climate is," Persson said.

"I could have understood it when interest rates were at 500 percent (during a 1992 financial crisis) but not now when we have state finances in order and companies are making big profits. I don't know what they base their arguments on," he added.
Swedish mobile phone giant Ericsson joined a growing chorus of companies at the weekend which say a poor business climate and crushing taxation may force them to move operations overseas.
In a radio interview, Ericsson's chief executive Lars Ramqvist said the company board had decided to look into a possible move of the Stockholm head office.

"The investigation should be seen in the light that only three percent of our business is in Sweden," Ramqvist said. "In addition, the owners would like to see how we can recruit managers to Ericsson in the long-term."
"For tax reasons it is almost hopeless to get a foreigner to move here," he told the radio. Highly paid employees routinely pay 60 percent of their salaries in tax.
"If politicians don't understand that we must reward development and competence, Ericsson won't manage the restructuring we are facing," Ramqvist said.
Persson, head of a centre-left Social Democratic government which has for years had a prickly relationship with the country's powerful business leaders, accused them of playing politics.
He said some of the companies threatening to quit Sweden had been regularly posting record profits.
Persson said an article in a newspaper in which 100 managing directors slammed the government's decision to phase out nuclear power was a case in point of business leaders playing politics.
But Persson hinted at a compromise by saying he was looking at tax relief for key foreign employees working in Sweden.
Junior Finance Minister Thomas Ostros, who deals with taxation issues, rejected Ericsson's complaints in a newspaper article on Tuesday, saying the corporate climate in Sweden was exceptionally good.
"Where else can they find a country with the kind of labour force we have, with labour market stability, with little bureaucracy and in addition get low mortgages," Ostros said.
Neighbouring Finland and other European countries have special tax rules for foreigners.
